    How this workspace works
    To use the bundled database, enter tinydb people.db in Command and choose Run. The prompt supplies an example INSERT and SELECT. Leave TinyDB returns to the C workspace commands.
    The compiler builds each C program into WebAssembly and runs it on your device. Files share one workspace with no subdirectory paths. It supports arguments, preloaded standard input, multiple C sources, and local headers. It does not provide a Unix shell, pipes, networking, or native Linux executables. Use Browser Linux for native tools and threads.
    The TinyDB prompt runs the included C program for each statement against the same file. INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE, and COUNT are supported for the people table; each successful mutation commits immediately. It is a teaching database with 128 rows, scans, and a bounded binary format. It has no transactions, indexes, concurrent writers, or crash-durability guarantee. Its source also runs as a stdin REPL in Browser Linux.
    Files save in this browser using IndexedDB. Download important files; clearing site data removes them. Files are separate from lesson drafts and completion. Limits: 32 files, 2 MB per file, 8 MB total, 256 KB per C source, 100 KB output, and 5 seconds per run (up to 2 minutes to prepare the compiler). Stopping or trapping retains the files from before the command. A normal nonzero exit still saves file changes.
    Learn C by building a database
    Start with a small C program and work toward TinyDB. The first chapter assumes no C experience.

    ← Chapter 11: Correctness and Big O
    How does the work grow?
    Search a sorted list of integers for its last value. Count one comparison each time we inspect an element.
    Linear search checks every element. Binary search repeatedly halves the remaining range.
    Try a larger list
    For this example, doubling the list doubles linear search’s comparisons, while binary search needs one extra comparison. This illustrates linear O(n) and logarithmic O(log n) growth. Both iterative searches use O(1) extra space.
    Other growth rates and formal notation
    Big O describes an asymptotic upper bound, not an exact runtime. We also use Θ for a tight asymptotic bound and Ω for a lower bound. Always specify the input size, assumptions, and case being analyzed.
    GrowthExample
    O(1)Read one array element by index
    O(log n)Binary search: worst-case time on sorted data
    O(n)Scan an entire array
    O(n log n)Merge sort: worst-case time
    O(n²)Insertion sort: worst-case time
    These growth classes omit constant factors. Algorithm, input order, implementation, and hardware affect actual timings. Auxiliary space is analyzed separately.

    ← Complete course
    Everything runs in your browser
    The course uses two browser environments. Neither requires an account or local installation.
    Inline C and the command workspace
    Run compatible C examples directly in each lesson. Drafts and lesson marks stay in this browser. Inline program files last for one run. The command workspace keeps files between successful runs and supports file import and download.
    Browser Linux
    Use Browser Linux for all Part 8 concurrency lessons, GCC/Clang compiler experiments, multi-file projects, files, and optional GDB investigations. Choose Start Linux to load the terminal inside the course. GCC, GDB, Make, Python, and nano are already installed.
    1. Open Browser Linux from your lesson and choose Run lab in Linux.
    2. Wait for Linux is ready and inspect the selected command’s output.
    3. Use Edit a course file in this browser, then Run edited source in Linux.
    4. Export a work archive before stopping or reloading.
    Its filesystem is temporary. Import a downloaded work backup into a new session to continue. The course keeps the current terminal alive while you move between course pages, but closing or reloading the site ends that session.
    Reading documentation
    Finding and reading C documentation teaches reference contracts. Use the online links in each lesson. Manual commands are optional reference examples for systems with installed manual pages; the Browser Linux image does not include those pages.
    Optional tooling notes
    ThreadSanitizer is optional reading, with no extra lab or installation required. The browser course teaches concurrency using working Linux threads, synchronization, and invariant checks. Emulator timings do not establish multicore performance or real-device durability.
    What the projects provide
    The bundle contains the complete worked examples, two editable Part 2 projects, and the broken GDB programs with separate references. Later chapter workshops extend and assemble bounded database models; they do not imply a production database is already complete.

    Browser lab · Linux terminal
    Browser Linux
    This terminal includes the compiler, debugger, and threads used by the course. No account or local installation is required. Choose Start Linux below to load it.
    1. Start the prepared Linux workspace
    The course prepares GCC, Clang, GDB, Make, Python, nano and the example files automatically. Choose Start Linux and wait for Linux is ready. The guest uses 1 GiB of memory, plus browser overhead. Its x86 Linux target has 32-bit pointers.
    Download course source bundle (optional)
    2. Run the selected lab
    Choose Run lab in Linux. The page sends the selected command to Linux; inspect its output in the terminal.
    Initial failures in unfinished projects and debugging starters are deliberate. Your lesson identifies its source files and checks. Use the source editor below or nano path/to/file.c in the terminal. In nano, Ctrl+O then Enter saves; Ctrl+X exits.
    Edit a course file in this browser
    The page saves your edits as a browser draft automatically. Select a source file, edit it, then choose Run edited source in Linux. That action replaces the selected guest source with the current editor text and runs the selected lab. You do not need to download or upload editor changes.
    Open this section to load the course C sources.
    Bring a Linux-edited file back into this editor
    This editor starts with the course original or its own browser draft. After restoring a Linux backup, export the guest file before editing it here, then use Import source file for the selected path:
    Edits here are separate from the guest until you choose Run edited source in Linux. Import source file changes the browser draft; it does not overwrite the guest immediately.
    The Linux system has not been loaded.
    The terminal, emulator, firmware, kernel and guest files are served by this course. Runtime sources and licences.
    3. Save before closing
    The terminal filesystem is temporary. After creating ~/work/c-foundry, run this to download your sources, generated files, and edits:
    Restore a downloaded work backup
    In a fresh Linux session, use its upload control to import c-foundry-work.tar.gz. Choose Restore uploaded archive to send the restore command to the terminal:
    Restore into a fresh session. Unpacking the original course bundle over edited files can replace those edits. Files exported from this terminal can also be imported into the browser command workspace where their format is supported.

    UNDER THE HOOD
    A real browser C lab.
    Clang and LLD are compiled to WebAssembly. Your source compiles and runs locally in a Web Worker. No compilation server is involved.
    The browser uses the experimental wasm-clang toolchain. It supports C17 and a subset of WASI. Native processes, sockets, and some system APIs are unavailable. Programs have a 5-second execution limit; standard input is provided before running.
    The page saves source, input, and completed lessons when browser storage is available. Lesson-run files are temporary; the command workspace saves files in this browser. Output checks compare the program’s results with the supplied cases.
